episode_title: Seven Stories That Should Be Films

stories.topic: The Funeral That Raised a Question: Bacha Khan's Servants of God
stories.summary: In 1988, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, known as Bacha Khan or the 'Sarhadi Gandhi', died in Peshawar. Tens of thousands of people, joined by the Afghan president, followed his body to Jalalabad for burial. He had founded the Khudai Khidmatgar ('servants of God') in 1930. It grew from about a thousand members to 25,000 a year later, and eventually to lakhs of red-kurta-wearing marchers, the 'Red Shirts'. They met every provocation with principled nonviolence. Gandhi first saw in him a kindred soul and later an inspiration. The movement opposed Partition, then asked for a Pashtun homeland, then chose to stay in Pakistan, where the state crushed it: members were jailed or killed and the movement faded away. Bacha Khan died a lonely old man, yet ordinary people still turned out in huge numbers to mourn him.
stories.insight: A state can erase a movement from politics and still fail to erase it from people's memory. Amit's broader point is that once a state decides the direction everyone must go in, free thinkers become its first casualties.
stories.quote: Yeah, the state might have forgotten you and cast you away, but it still means something to the common people.

stories.topic: Underwear and Turbans: The Akalis Who Inspired a Pathan
stories.summary: In the 1920s, Bacha Khan was in a British jail alongside Akali prisoners. The jailers ordered the Akalis to take off their turbans, which their faith forbade. Instead they stripped down to their underwear, kept only their turbans on, and chanted 'Sar jaave taan jaave, mera Sikhi dharam na jaave' ('let my head go, but not my Sikh faith'). Bacha Khan watched this and was deeply moved. In jail he also met figures like Baba Kharak Singh of the Akali Dal.
stories.insight: Courage spreads across communities. A Muslim Pathan learned something about principled defiance from Sikh prisoners, which is one small example of how India's freedom movements drew inspiration from each other.
stories.quote: I mean it's not his faith, but it is faith, it is principles, it is fighting against authority and oppression.

stories.topic: Mukulika Banerjee's Question That Kept Her Up at Night
stories.summary: As a PhD student in India in the late 1980s, Mukulika Banerjee was puzzled. Academic convention held that peasants don't do mass politics and that Pathans are a violent frontier people. So how did a Pathan who grew up among peasants lead the subcontinent's greatest nonviolent movement? An advisor told her to do a PhD only if she had a question that kept her up at night. She did. Indian institutions repeatedly refused to back a woman going to the North-West Frontier Province, and she spent two years hunting for funding before some came, partly from abroad. She then learned Pashto, wore a chador, went village to village looking for surviving Khudai Khidmatgars, and took ten years to write 'The Pathan Unarmed'.
stories.insight: The best research starts from a burning question that contradicts received wisdom. The obstacles thrown up by gatekeepers are part of the price of answering it.
stories.quote: Only do a PhD if you have a question that keeps you up at night, which you are desperate to answer.

stories.topic: The Expensive Chicken and the Beef
stories.summary: During her fieldwork, Mukulika found that beef was the everyday staple in Pashtun villages, but every household kept one expensive chicken to serve honoured guests as an act of hospitality. She didn't want families to sacrifice that chicken everywhere she went, so she started eating beef with them. Much later she told her devout Hindu mother. Amit calls her mother's response a beautiful story that moves him deeply.
stories.insight: Real respect for another culture can mean giving up a taboo of your own so that you don't impose costs on your hosts. It also shows that people back home can be more open-minded than we expect.
stories.quote: every household has an expensive chicken that they keep and they give it to their honored guests

stories.topic: The Street of Storytellers, Visited Unknowingly
stories.summary: In 2006 Amit visited Kissa Khwani Bazaar in Peshawar, loved its look and its people, took photographs, and wrote a blog post called 'Twilight in the Street of Storytellers'. Only later did he learn that around 200 people had been killed in a massacre there, the Khudai Khidmatgar movement's equivalent of Jallianwala Bagh.
stories.insight: We often walk through places without knowing the history in them. Knowing it turns a pretty bazaar into a site of memory.
stories.quote: I had no idea of the history of this place, how resonant it was. I just thought that it looks fantastic. I love the people here

stories.topic: The Fat Frogs of Tatsinskaya
stories.summary: About 250,000 German troops were encircled at Stalingrad. They needed 700 to 900 tons of supplies a day, 300 tons was the bare survival minimum, and the airlift actually delivered only 100 to 150 tons. A year earlier, roughly 100,000 men trapped near Leningrad had been kept alive by air, so Hitler's team tried the same thing. Transports carrying about 2.5 tons each flew 1.5-hour sorties out of Tatsinskaya, the airfield closest to the action, about 80 km inside German-held territory. Following their doctrine of hitting the enemy's logistics, the Soviets sent a near-suicidal tank raid through thin German lines. Scouts gave only ten minutes' warning. Planes tried to take off with too little fuel and crashed into each other. T-34s parked at the edge of the runway and shot planes down one by one as they lifted off. Of roughly 200 planes, about 70 were destroyed. The surviving planes had to fly from a farther airfield, the airlift collapsed, and weeks later Paulus surrendered.
stories.insight: Huge outcomes can turn on a small, clever blow against logistics. Ajay sees the planners behind the raid as the real heroes, and he thinks a film should match Dunkirk's restraint and let the events themselves supply the drama.
stories.quote: the tanks were like, you know, fat frogs grabbing one drone ant at a time.

stories.topic: The Bridge: When Military Police Shot Their Own
stories.summary: The Red Army covered roughly 2,500 km from Stalingrad to Berlin in about 500 days, about the distance from Ludhiana to Kanyakumari. About ten times along the way, a retreating German army, with all its men, equipment and stores, had to squeeze across a single bridge. Artillery then was too imprecise to easily destroy such bridges, so they held, but each crossing was a brutal planning problem: what to abandon, and how many vehicles of what kind could get across per day. Tired, frightened men under fire tended to break ranks and turn into a mob, and then the crossing collapsed. At several of these crossings, German military police killed German soldiers to keep order.
stories.insight: A chokepoint under pressure is an operations problem, and the panic of the people in it can destroy the very capacity they need to escape. Holding discipline there can become a matter of life and death.
stories.quote: at several of these bridge crossings, the German military police killed German soldiers so as to hold the discipline.

stories.topic: Haimabati Sen: Child Widow to Doctor
stories.summary: Haimabati was born in 1866 in a poor family in Khulna, then part of Bengal and now in Bangladesh, to a father who was progressive for his time. During the 1872 famine, aged six, she was caught stealing rice from the family store to give to the starving poor outside. A visiting sub-inspector found that she was the only child in her school who could answer his question, and told her that so much learning was a sure route to widowhood. Her relatives were appalled when she read the Ramayana. At nine she was married to a 45-year-old widower who had two children her own age. She played with their dolls by day and was traumatised at night. Her husband died when she was ten. By twelve her parents and in-laws were dead too, and an uncle took the money left for her. Many child widows of that era ended up in prostitution; one 1853 Kolkata study counted more than 12,000 prostitutes, many of them child widows. Haimabati instead made her way to Benares, educated herself, became a doctor, remarried and had children. As Amit recalls, she later became a prominent figure among doctors, and something of a sharp-tongued one.
stories.insight: Child marriage, huge age gaps and short life expectancy together made child widowhood common. Her escape from that system was nearly impossible, which is what makes her story so extraordinary.
stories.quote: And this twelve year old child widow from this village in Bengal goes to Benares, educates herself, becomes a doctor, gets married again, has kids again.

stories.topic: The Memoir Locked in a Trunk for Eighty Years
stories.summary: Haimabati began writing her memoirs in the 1920s and died in 1933. The papers sat locked in a trunk for about eighty years. When they surfaced, her family didn't grasp their importance until Tapan Raychaudhuri persuaded them, and the memoir was edited, translated and published. Amit pictures the opening shot of his web series as a woman's hand opening that dusty trunk, intercut with a little girl's feet running and stumbling. He would add a fictional parallel story about a modern descendant who finds the papers.
stories.insight: Much of history survives by luck, and an extraordinary woman's voice can almost be lost to a forgotten trunk. Amit is baffled that stories like this aren't already being filmed.
stories.quote: Everybody can read the story of her life in her words, right? And imagine being locked in a trunk for eighty years

stories.topic: Indira's Letter to Sanjay
stories.summary: Coomi Kapoor's book reproduces a private letter Indira Gandhi wrote to Sanjay in the late 1960s, in which she essentially says they care only about power, not left or right. Amit reads the Congress's leftward turn of that period, including bank nationalisation, as a tactic to set her apart from her rivals in the Syndicate, such as Morarji Desai, rather than as ideology. He contrasts her with Nehru, who acted on conviction. Still, he declines to simply judge her: at 13, her aunt Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit called her ugly and stupid, which reportedly left a deep mark.
stories.insight: Policies that hurt millions can come from political tactics rather than conviction. And even people who wield power ruthlessly are shaped by old wounds.
stories.quote: she essentially says that we don't care about left or right, we only care about power.

stories.topic: Vidya Charan Shukla and the Editors Who Crawled
stories.summary: As Information and Broadcasting minister during the Emergency, Vidya Charan Shukla called Delhi's editors to his office and told them: not one bad word against Indira Gandhi. Apart from exceptions like Ramnath Goenka's Indian Express, most complied. Simon Jenkins said he had seen Franco's Spain and Mao's China but never a press crackdown like this one. S. Nihal Singh described a Times of India editor who followed every order during the Emergency and then, once it ended, wrote a two-page piece attacking Indira. Shukla was a sycophant who wanted her made ruler for life with no further elections, and he was accused of harassing actresses. Amit compares him to Gollum, enslaved by his lust for power. In 2013, old and long irrelevant, Shukla was killed in a Naxal attack on his way to a Congress rally. Amit admits he found it hard to feel sad.
stories.insight: Compliant media and opportunistic hypocrites show up under every authoritarian turn. Amit leaves it to viewers to draw the parallels with today.
stories.quote: in LK Advani's memorable words, when asked to bend, they chose to crawl.

stories.topic: Peepli, 1976: The Women Making Cow-Dung Cakes
stories.summary: During Sanjay Gandhi's sterilisation drive, some hospitals refused to admit pregnant women unless they could show a nasbandi certificate. In Peepli, a Haryana village under Bansi Lal (who elsewhere had a protesting elderly advocate stripped and paraded through town), an ageing widower named Hawa Lal was taken away to meet sterilisation quotas and died during the operation. The village erupted. Officials came back with soldiers and grabbed the first man they saw, a cobbler, for forced sterilisation. People from neighbouring villages joined the protests, and hundreds of police laid siege to the village. At 6 AM shots were fired, killing two women who were making cow-dung cakes outside. The rest of the village then submitted to the nasbandi.
stories.insight: Quotas enforced by a coercive state turn into atrocities. Amit would tell this story by first showing the victims as full human beings, so that the viewer feels their deaths as lives cut short and not as statistics.
stories.quote: show them as actual human beings with dreams, with aspirations, with hundreds of stories within them, a life to live

stories.topic: Snehalata Reddy's Crime Was Friendship
stories.summary: Snehalata Reddy was a cultured actress in theatre and film with a deep love of poetry. Her husband, as Amit recalls, was a poet and filmmaker. Her only crime was being a friend of George Fernandes, who was on the run. She was arrested and treated badly, and she was not allowed treatment for her asthma. By one account she went in a young beautiful woman and came out looking old and haggard. Shortly after her release at the end of the Emergency, she died of a heart attack.
stories.insight: Authoritarian regimes punish people for who they know, not just what they do. Artists in particular must either sing the regime's tune or pay the price.
stories.quote: And her crime was she was a friend of George Fernandes who was on the run.

stories.topic: Babu Beats Bobby
stories.summary: In 1977, the government was nervous about a JP Narayan rally where Jagjivan Ram, nicknamed 'Babu', was to speak. It told Doordarshan to broadcast the blockbuster 'Bobby' (1973) to keep people at home. The rally was packed anyway, and the next day's headline read 'Babu Beats Bobby'. Amit would open his Emergency web series by intercutting a nervous, portly politician putting on his cap backstage with a family huddled around a 1970s TV watching Dimple Kapadia.
stories.insight: Distracting people with entertainment fails once people are angry enough. A single headline can capture the moment a regime loses its hold.
stories.quote: And the headline in the newspaper the next day was Babu beats Bobby.

stories.topic: A Note Dropped From a Prison Van
stories.summary: Journalist Virendra Kapoor, Coomi Kapoor's husband, was being moved between jails in a police van. He scribbled a note (a parchi) for Coomi with her landline number, saying which station he'd be at so she could see him, and dropped it out of the back. A man on a scooter behind the van saw it, waited until the van was out of sight, picked it up, and got the message to her. She went to Bareilly to see him being put on a train with three other prisoners, not knowing if she'd ever see him again. At the other end of the same platform, a crowd was chanting slogans for a Congress politician boarding the train.
stories.insight: Small acts of decency by strangers kept people connected under repression. In the same scene, the powerful carried on celebrating a few metres away.
stories.quote: And at the same time, and the scene is so cinematic

stories.topic: Subramanian Swamy's Disguise and the Young Karyakarta
stories.summary: While on the run during the Emergency, Subramanian Swamy disguised himself as a Sardar, with a pagri and kara. One of his hideouts was Ahmedabad, since Gujarat did not have a Congress government then. He stayed with Makarand Desai, and the RSS karyakarta who met him at the station and escorted him to the house was Narendra Modi. Other dissenters of the time also went on to big political careers: Arun Jaitley, then a young law student, went to jail, and Lalu Prasad Yadav and Nitish Kumar were young activists in JP's movement.
stories.insight: The Emergency was a crucible for much of today's political class. Amit says that if he had been one of those young dissenters, he would have resolved to treat the opposition and the press with dignity if he ever held power, and he is not sure that lesson has been learned.
stories.quote: That RSS karyakarta was Narendra Modi.

stories.topic: Govind Nihalani, My Friend Sancho, and an Accidental Ghosting
stories.summary: After Amit's 2009 novel 'My Friend Sancho' came out, filmmaker Govind Nihalani, director of 'Ardh Satya' and 'Party', wanted to make a film of it. Amit wrote a treatment note, but nobody in Bollywood bit. Around 2010, Nihalani told him that nothing would happen in the Hindi film industry, but the Marathi industry reminded him of Hindi alternative cinema in the early 1980s, when Shyam Benegal and others were at their peak. He suggested moving the story to Pune. Amit wrote a two-pager, the project stalled, and out of embarrassment he stopped meeting Nihalani. He apologises on air.
stories.insight: Creative energy moves between film industries over time. On the personal side, ghosting someone often comes from embarrassment rather than malice, and it gets harder to undo the longer it lasts.
stories.quote: once you realize that you've ghosted someone, it's very difficult to go back and say that, you know, I'm sorry, I didn't mean to do that

stories.topic: A Mad Love Story: Ajay's Parents
stories.summary: Ajay's parents had an inter-caste marriage. They eloped three times, and the first two attempts ended in terrible, violent events. On the third, they kept running until they reached Banaras, where they secretly married in an Arya Samaj ceremony. Their story was once optioned for a film but never made.
stories.insight: Behind many settled lives is an earlier generation that took real risks. Some of the most dramatic stories sit inside our own families.
stories.quote: they eloped three times. The first two times were terrible, violent events, and then they ran and ran and did not stop running till they reached Banaras.

stories.topic: Writing Darkness at Noon as France Fell
stories.summary: In 1940 Arthur Koestler, a Hungarian who wrote in German, was living in a dingy part of Paris with his girlfriend Daphne Hardy, a 21-year-old British art student. He wrote the novel page by page in German and she translated it into English as he went. Her German was shaky and she knew little about Soviet communism, so she softened things: for example, she rendered 'interrogation' as 'hearing'. But she was living with him, talking with him, and had a feel for the book. Then the Germans reached Paris, France surrendered, and Koestler, wanted in many countries, was interned. He survived only because the Germans never worked out who he was. Before they split up, he posted the German manuscript to his editor in Switzerland. Hardy, a British citizen, hid the dangerous English manuscript and was evacuated from Marseille. Koestler escaped, Ajay thinks by walking across the Pyrenees into Spain.
stories.insight: A book that changed the world came close to being lost, and its survival depended on luck and on one person's courage. Ajay adds a wry policy point: the absence of good identity systems saved a dissident's life.
stories.quote: the only reason he got away was because of bad identity infrastructure.

stories.topic: Daphne Hardy Names the Book
stories.summary: Koestler's working title was a dull 'Rubashov: A Novel'. In England, with a war on, no phones and Koestler out of reach, Hardy sold the English manuscript to a publisher and retitled it herself: 'Darkness at Noon'. The book became hugely influential. Ajay argues it tipped the 1946 French election, which the Communist Party lost because readers finally understood what Soviet Russia really was.
stories.insight: A translator's bold call on a title helped shape one of the 20th century's most consequential books, and a novel helped shift a country's election.
stories.quote: Hey there was a war going on, he was out of reach, there were no phones, and she chose the title Darkness at Noon.

stories.topic: The German Original Resurfaces in 2015
stories.summary: For 75 years the world had only Hardy's translation. In 2015 the German manuscript turned up in Switzerland, and the graduate student who found it immediately understood what it was. A new translation followed, informed by the Kremlin archives that were briefly open before Putin's Russia closed up again, so the new translator could check Koestler's insider knowledge of Stalin's interrogations against the archival record. Ajay holds up his two most prized possessions: a 1941 edition that came from his father, and the 2015 edition.
stories.insight: Rediscovered manuscripts and newly opened archives together can give us a clearer version of a classic. Comparing the two translations shows what the first one got right and what it softened.
stories.quote: So, dear reader, I commend you please read these books, and you know what? Read both versions.

recommendations.creator: Mukulika Banerjee
recommendations.context: The heart of Amit's first web-series pitch, which follows Mukulika's ten-year journey to write this book alongside Bacha Khan's own story.
recommendations.reason: It answers how Pathan peasants built the subcontinent's greatest nonviolent movement. Her answer is that Bacha Khan rooted it in the Islamic idea of the greater inner jihad and in the Pashtun codes of courage, hospitality and refuge. This overturns the stereotypes about both Pathans and peasants.

recommendations.item: The Incredible Curiosities of Mukulika Banerjee (Episode 276, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit first imagined the web series while recording this episode, and he points listeners to it for the details.
recommendations.reason: It has the full story of her fight for funding, her fieldwork in the North-West Frontier Province, and the beef-and-chicken story.

recommendations.creator: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
recommendations.context: Mentioned while describing Bacha Khan's years in jail with Akali prisoners and Baba Kharak Singh.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great autobiography. It shows a period when the finest minds were in jail rather than in universities, and how those encounters shaped Bacha Khan.

recommendations.item: Twilight in the Street of Storytellers
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2006 blog post and photographs from Peshawar's Kissa Khwani Bazaar.
recommendations.reason: A record of a place he loved before he knew it had been the scene of a massacre on the scale of Jallianwala Bagh.

recommendations.creator: Kavitha Rao
recommendations.context: Where Amit first read about Haimabati Sen.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a great book by an excellent writer, about 19th-century women doctors who were all remarkable, because a woman had to be remarkable even to become one.

recommendations.item: Kavitha Rao and Our Lady Doctors (Episode 235, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's conversation with Kavitha Rao, mentioned in the Haimabati chapter.
recommendations.reason: The long-form conversation behind the book that introduced him to Haimabati.

recommendations.item: The Memoirs of Dr Haimabati Sen
recommendations.creator: Geraldine Forbes and Tapan Raychaudhuri (editors)
recommendations.context: The memoir that sat in a trunk for eighty years before it was translated and published.
recommendations.reason: It tells, in her own words, how a destitute child widow became a doctor. It is now available in print and on Kindle.

recommendations.item: Devangshu Datta Traded His Corduroy Pants (Episode 348, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Ajay's bridge story reminded Amit of it.
recommendations.reason: Devangshu reveals that three of his great-grandfathers had institutions named after them and the fourth was a dhoti-clad river pirate in Bengal. Amit thinks there's a movie in that too.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Recommended to listeners curious about Ajay's love of military strategy.
recommendations.reason: A five-and-a-half-hour 'masterclass' from Ajay, who has also lectured Indian Army generals on strategy.

recommendations.item: The State of the Ukraine War (Episode 14, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned as the follow-up to the long Ukraine episode.
recommendations.reason: An update on the war from the same military-strategy lens Ajay brings to the eastern-front stories here.

recommendations.creator: Coomi Kapoor
recommendations.context: The source for Amit's Emergency web-series pitch and most of its characters and stories.
recommendations.reason: Amit adores it and thinks everyone should read it, both for this period and to understand the fundamental nature of the Indian state and the damage its power can do, because history rhymes in disturbing ways.

recommendations.item: Coomi Kapoor Has the Inside Track (Episode 305, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions he has done an episode with Coomi Kapoor.
recommendations.reason: A long conversation with the author whose firsthand account of the Emergency Amit relies on.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned before discussing Sanjay Gandhi's sterilisation drive.
recommendations.reason: Their earlier argument for why population density is good and sterilisation is a worse kind of coercion.

recommendations.context: The idea behind Amit's novel concept 'Missing', about a boy who wakes up to find all of humanity gone.
recommendations.reason: It frames the question of who we are once there is no one left to reflect us back.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2009 novel, which Govind Nihalani wanted to adapt into a film.
recommendations.reason: Amit dismisses it as slight. It comes up as the start of his story about Nihalani, Marathi cinema, and the apology he owes.

recommendations.creator: Christopher Nolan
recommendations.context: Ajay explains that this episode began with Dunkirk: watching it felt like being taken back in a time machine.
recommendations.reason: Amit, who says he is no Nolan fanboy, calls it the best war film ever made. Ajay sees it as the model for letting real events carry the drama.

recommendations.creator: Arthur Koestler
recommendations.context: The subject of Ajay's final chapter, about how the book was written, lost and rediscovered.
recommendations.reason: It goes inside the minds of Soviet leaders confessing at show trials. Ajay says it changed the world, including the 1946 French election. He urges reading both Daphne Hardy's original translation and the 2015 translation of the rediscovered German manuscript.

recommendations.creator: Stefan Zweig
recommendations.context: Amit's closing recommendation, prompted by Ajay's Koestler story.
recommendations.reason: Zweig's memoir of living through Europe's collapse into fascism, Bolshevism and nationalism. Amit reads out its 'pale horses of the apocalypse' passage.

core_ideas.explanation: Mukulika Banerjee found that Bacha Khan didn't import nonviolence. He reframed ideas his people already held: patience in Islam, the 'greater jihad' (Jihad-e-Akbar) as an inner struggle against fear and anger, and the Pashtun codes of ghairat (courage), melmastia (hospitality), badal (revenge) and nanawatai (refuge even for enemies). The British became unwanted guests who had broken the code of hospitality and had to be evicted politely but firmly. Because the ideology came from his followers' own culture, it was easy for them to understand and spread.
core_ideas.quote: The revolutionary ideology the Khudai Khidmatgars fashioned was thus rooted organically in their society and therefore readily communicable and comprehensible to its rank and file.

core_ideas.explanation: Indian freedom fighters are often said to have borrowed Western Enlightenment values. Amit argues that Indian culture holds opposite values side by side and can feed our worst instincts or our best ones. Liberal values also grow locally, if we look for them.
core_ideas.quote: And all of these beautiful values which come intellectually from the enlightenment also exist organically around us, if we just care to look hard enough.

core_ideas.concept: When the Best Minds Are in Jail
core_ideas.explanation: Under colonial rule, and later during the Emergency, prison was where leaders met, argued and were shaped. A government that jails its dissenters ends up locking away its best thinkers.
core_ideas.quote: there were periods of time where your best minds, your finest intellectuals were not in universities, they were not in think tanks, they were not in air conditioned cafes, they were in jails.

core_ideas.explanation: Soviet doctrine held that you defeat a modern army by choking its supplies, not by meeting it head-on. Tatsinskaya is the textbook case. Ajay notes that Ukraine is doing the same to Russian invaders today.
core_ideas.quote: The Soviet doctrine of war is you don't hit the enemy, you figure out their logistics and you hit the logistics. You choke the logistics.

core_ideas.concept: Owning a Plane vs. Having an Airworthy Plane
core_ideas.explanation: Planes must be light, so many parts are designed to wear out quickly and need frequent replacement. Flying more sorties means more maintenance and more downtime, so the number of aircraft you own overstates what you can actually fly.
core_ideas.quote: So it's one thing to own a plane. It's a different thing for that plane to be airworthy because every X kilometers, it's got to stop and get a lot of servicing done.

core_ideas.concept: Laminar vs. Turbulent Flow at a Chokepoint
core_ideas.explanation: A bridge is a pipe with fixed capacity. The most gets through when the flow is smooth and planned, with hard decisions made in advance about what to leave behind. Once desperate people turn into a mob, the flow becomes turbulent and the whole crossing breaks down.
core_ideas.quote: So to use a fluid mechanics analogy, what you want is a laminar flow and not a turbulent flow.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that labels like left and right hide what is really going on. Populism is a tactic of grabbing power by stirring up hatred of elites, and it looks the same whichever side uses it. Indira's power-first letter to Sanjay fits this pattern.
core_ideas.quote: Populism is the game of igniting the hatred against elites, and it's an evergreen strategy and it's wielded by the left or the right. But actually, at heart, it's the same.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit says the Emergency should be studied as a lesson in the oppressive power of the Indian state, not just as a closed chapter. The same patterns of pliant media, sycophantic ministers, jailed opponents and coercive targets can come back in new forms.
core_ideas.quote: it is dangerous to forget history. History, of course, as we know, doesn't repeat itself. It rhymes, but it rhymes in disturbing ways.

core_ideas.explanation: Anyone who suffered under, or resisted, abuse of power has the clearest reason to never repeat it: treat the opposition with dignity and let the press speak freely. Amit asks whether today's leaders, many of whom were Emergency-era dissenters, learned this.
core_ideas.quote: The lesson I would take from this is how dangerous power is. And I would determine to myself that if I am ever in power, I will be different.

core_ideas.explanation: Our sense of self is built from how others see us and how we want them to see us. Amit's novel idea 'Missing' runs two stories side by side. In one, a family finds that a missing person's absence becomes a strong presence in their lives. In the other, the missing boy wakes to find everyone else gone, which asks what a self is when there is no one left to mirror it.
core_ideas.quote: So if other people vanish, what is the self? You know, how does it shape itself? How does one live?

core_ideas.explanation: When the path is already laid out for you, you can arrive just by following it. When every barrier is against you, only exceptional people get through. That is why every 19th-century Indian woman doctor was remarkable.
core_ideas.quote: You know, a man could get there through inertia, just following the paths laid out. To be a woman and to do this was remarkable.

core_ideas.concept: Books in the Battle of Ideas
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay places Koestler and Orwell alongside Milton Friedman, Hayek and George Stigler in the 20th century's battle between liberal democracy and authoritarian or populist ideas. A novel like 'Darkness at Noon' could change how voters understood a regime. He thinks that battle is still not won.
core_ideas.quote: I feel even today so much about the basics of liberal democracy and authoritarian regimes has not been internalized by a lot of people.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay claims Amit will 'become one of the world's great movie makers, and we're actually giving away some of his concepts'. Amit: 'you left me speechless for a moment'.
After Amit's cinematic trunk-opening pitch, Ajay says: 'You see, I tell stories from history. This is the real thing. He's a movie maker.' Amit: 'No, no, I'm not a movie maker. I'm a lafunga.'
Ajay on the Bacha Khan pitch: 'I will sign up to watch this web series, even though I don't have a Netflix subscription.'
Amit, offering to be a showrunner: 'why do you just want to be a card carrying economist so boring?' Ajay: 'I am a happy customer.'
Amit on Ajay calling the tanks fat frogs: 'the last time you used that phrase fat frogs, you were asking me to lose weight. So I'm happier in this context.'
After hearing that Ajay's parents eloped three times: 'And out of that great romantic, courageous affair emerges a boring card carrying economist. What a waste. What a waste.'

Amit wore a red kurta in honour of the Khudai Khidmatgar 'Red Shirts' and asked Ajay to wear red, but Ajay had no red shirt. Amit's closing line: 'may some of these movies and web series get made, and we can also be celebrities and walk red carpets... You couldn't even wear a red shirt.'
On the 'Babu Beats Bobby' headline, Amit: 'it is just greatest fucking headline in independent India's history.'

Amit stumbles over Devangshu Datta's 'four grandfathers'. Ajay corrects him: 'Two grandfathers and four great grandfathers.' Then Amit muses about getting Devangshu to write down the memoirs of his river-pirate ancestor: 'Like how does one do that? What am I even saying?'
Ajay, Aadhaar-era policy wonk, on Koestler escaping because the Germans couldn't identify him: 'So, gentle reader, if you ever think that digital identity is such a great thing. Think twice.'
Amit's self-deprecation: 'I did write one shitty novel', and on his publisher V.K. Karthika of Westland, who agrees to publish every idea he pitches: 'I think she's kinda given up on me.'
Christopher Nolan's 'Dunkirk' (2017) inspired the episode. Ajay felt it was like being taken back in a time machine, and Amit calls it the best war film ever made.
'Sar jaave taan jaave, mera Sikhi dharam na jaave' ('let my head go, but not my Sikh faith'): the chant of the Akali prisoners who stripped to their underwear rather than remove their turbans.
Gandhi called Bacha Khan's movement the practical form of the idealistic nonviolence he believed in. Amit says Bacha Khan's 'God' in 'servants of God' is best read as a set of higher principles.
Kissa Khwani Bazaar in Peshawar, where around 200 people were killed, was the movement's Jallianwala Bagh.

Ajay's Indian yardsticks for wartime scale: a Tatsinskaya sortie is like a Bombay–Delhi or Bombay–Bhopal flight, and the Soviet march from Stalingrad to Berlin is like going from Ludhiana to Kanyakumari.
L.K. Advani on the press during the Emergency: 'when asked to bend, they chose to crawl.' Simon Jenkins said he had seen Franco's Spain and Mao's China but never such a press crackdown.
Amit compares Vidya Charan Shukla to Gollum from 'The Lord of the Rings', enslaved by his lust for power and ending up a pitiful figure.
A young Sanjay Gandhi stole hubcaps and Mercedes badges, back when people stuck the Mercedes logo on their Ambassadors and Fiats as a status symbol.
Emergency facts: Indira Gandhi jailed more people than the British did during the Quit India movement, and the entire Sanskrit department of Delhi University was put in jail.
Jailed dissenters, Arun Jaitley among them, crowded around the one transistor radio they had to catch the BBC, because Indian sources were telling them nothing.
Govind Nihalani, around 2010: the Marathi film industry reminded him of Hindi alternative cinema in the early 1980s, when Shyam Benegal and others were at their peak.
Ajay quotes Lionel Trilling: Koestler, Orwell and Camus 'lived at the dark crossroads of literature and politics'.

Stefan Zweig, read by Amit: 'All the pale horses of the apocalypse have stormed through my life. Revolution and famine, currency depreciation and terror, epidemics and emigration... and above all, the ultimate pestilence that has poisoned the flower of our European culture, nationalism in general.'
